extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, researchers, and scholars interested in the evaluation and reform of peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and critique of journal and grant peer-review processes, including empirical findings about bias, reviewer competence, editorial responsibilities, and alternative funding models. Focuses on how review practices affect publication and funding decisions and scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: "Peer review is the procedure that governs access to publication and money in modern science. Its function is to identify and reject poor work, to improve and accept good work, and to let the best through unimpeded.","It performs the first two of these purposes reasonably well but fails disastrously with the third.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite function as a baseline for assessing peer-review systems; recognize that systems may succeed at quality control and improvement but fail to ensure the best work is propagated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing reduces bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence: the Modern Language Association instituted blind reviewing and "the result was unequivocal: There was a dramatic rise in the acceptance of papers by female authors." Peters & Ceci produced similar evidence about institutional prestige effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement or test blind review to mitigate gender and institutional prestige bias, while noting that author identity can sometimes still be inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer competence, accuracy, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed reviewer breakdown (Horrobin): about one-third of referees' reports are accurate, comment on important issues, and are fair; about one-third are accurate but obsessed with the trivial; about one-third are inaccurate and demonstrably so. Many reports are couched in intemperate language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reviewers for substantive competence and fairness; monitor and address abusive or irrelevant criticism. Competence rates should inform editorial assignment and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Built-in bias against highly innovative work
rubrics_metrics.description: "The referee system as currently constituted is a disaster. What is most disastrous is its built-in bias against highly innovative work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert that conventional review procedures may preferentially suppress radical or paradigm-challenging submissions; consider safeguards to protect innovative research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor control and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some form of review is necessary... It must, however, be controlled by a strong and open-minded editor who is prepared to edit and not blindly act on the recommendations of referees."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should actively supervise refereeing, perform substantive editorial judgment, and be willing to override or synthesize referee recommendations rather than follow them automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review for funding differs from publication
rubrics_metrics.description: "Peer review of proposed research involves a prediction of the potential value of the proposed project... The ability of principal investigators to conduct the research effectively in their institutional settings and to analyze and interpret the results meaningfully is an essential feature of the grant peer-review process."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design grant review criteria to assess PI competence, institutional resources, and feasibility; do not conflate publication-review criteria with grant-review criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel-based review increases reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF practice: reviews typically involve four to six written reviews plus discussion by a panel of five to ten scientists, "increasing the reliability of the process substantially."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where reliability is critical (e.g., funding), use more reviewers and structured panel discussion rather than only two isolated reviewers to reduce random variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious institutions can bias evaluative studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique: using completely fictitious institution names (e.g., Tri-Valley Center for Human Potential) may "virtually ensure an initial negative affect" and confound conclusions about prestige-based bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimentally testing reviewer bias, prefer real lower-prestige institution names or otherwise validate that the manipulation isolates prestige rather than novelty/legitimacy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low interreferee agreement and inherent subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation in physics: "In only about 10-15% of cases do two referees agree on acceptance or rejection the first time around" (even with identities known). Acceptance rates vary widely across journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect substantial reviewer disagreement; factor interrater variability into editorial processes and into interpretations of individual reviewer recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and institutional affiliation as heuristics (controversial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument: institution and reputation are legitimate measures of the value of work; "When I scale our experience... it boggles the mind that anyone could ever imagine that 'objective' selection criteria could exist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the pragmatic role of reputational heuristics while weighing ethical and epistemic concerns about bias; field norms may differ on legitimacy of such heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to dishonesty and conflicts in grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are strong reasons to believe that because the stakes are so high many of [reviewers] are dishonest and deliberately shoot down work that is in any way threatening to their own personal research lines."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement conflict-of-interest checks, transparency, and oversight in grant review to reduce strategic rejection and protect fair competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative funding models to reduce peer-review corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal: abolish the grant system; (1) give accredited universities capital grants based on student numbers for infrastructure, (2) give academics small annual grants (~$20,000) to enable research; additionally, governments should offer graded cash prizes for practical solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional funding and prize mechanisms as complements or alternatives to competitive peer-reviewed grants to reduce perverse incentives and protect blue-sky research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flawed-masterpiece hypothesis (risk vs. error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative explanation to ascription: high-risk (innovative) papers are more likely to contain errors or controversial claims and therefore to provoke unfavorable referee responses — i.e., some manuscripts are 'flawed masterpieces.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting rejection of innovative work, consider whether rejections reflect substantive flaws rather than solely prestige bias; selection systems should distinguish error from novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish manuscripts with low interrater agreement to foster innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mahoney's suggestion (Note 1): conceiving publication of manuscripts that elicit the least reliable ratings (lowest interrater agreement) would favor manuscripts with one enthusiastic reviewer and another rejecting, potentially signaling robust, provocative contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with publication criteria that value divergent reviewer opinions as indicators of heuristic or frontier work, balancing risk of error against potential payoff of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection/sample bias due to citation levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Peters & Ceci's sample: the 12 resubmitted papers were "above average in their citation levels" which could reflect either author eminence (ascription) or that the papers were recognized as minor masterpieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control for citation-based selection effects when designing studies of peer review; high citation could confound analyses of prestige versus intrinsic paper quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human factors and tacit biases in manuscript assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers are influenced by first impressions, prestige, 'clean-ness' of typed copy, writing style, timeliness, prior publication claims, and other tacit cues that ideally should not determine judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and attempt to mitigate cognitive and contextual biases (e.g., via reviewer training, standardized evaluation checklists, blind review where feasible, and conscientious editorial oversight).
